old: Long before it meant anything small and crawling, this word named something that haunted people in the dark — a scarecrow or hobgoblin.
By the 1600s it had settled onto a small biting pest that shares its bed with you at night.
Its insect sense may owe something to a lookalike word, budde, which is also kin to the word "bud."
clues: This casual name for a small creature once haunted nightmares instead: centuries ago it meant a scarecrow or hobgoblin, possibly from a Celtic root for goblins.
It's a loose, everyday catch-all for any creepy-crawly, broader than 'insect', and also names a glitch in software. That machine-error sense was used well before the famous computer moth.
Spies plant one to eavesdrop, you can catch a stomach one, and a cozy child is snug as one in a rug.
